tours.title: Song-Kul Horse Trek & Yurt Stay
tours.summary: Three days on horseback across a 3,400 m pass to Song-Kul lake, with two nights in herder family yurts.
description: Ride from the village of Kyzart over summer pastures (jailoo) and the Jalgyz Karagai pass to Song-Kul, a lake at 3,016 m where herder families set up their yurts from June to September.
You sleep in family yurts, eat what the hosts cook and ride with a local horseman who sets the pace. No riding experience is needed: the horses are calm and used to the trail.

faqs.question: Do I need riding experience?
faqs.answer: No. The horses walk in a line behind the horseman, who controls the pace. Confident riders can trot on the flat meadows by the lake.

faqs.question: How hard is the altitude?
faqs.answer: You cross a 3,400 m pass and sleep at about 3,000 m. Most people feel only mild breathlessness. Spend a night in Bishkek or Kochkor first and drink plenty of water.

faqs.question: What are the toilets and charging like?
faqs.answer: Toilets are simple outhouses near the camp. Some camps have solar power in the evening; bring a power bank.

faqs.question: Is there phone signal?
faqs.answer: There is little or no signal at Song-Kul. Your guide can reach the camp hosts and the operator.

reviews.author: Clara L.
reviews.body: The horses were steady even on the steep descent, and Bakyt took great care of us. Sleeping in a warm yurt with horses grazing outside was the highlight of our trip.

reviews.author: Marcus W.
reviews.body: Paying a small deposit online and the rest in Kochkor was simple. The food was hearty. Bring a warm jacket: it gets cold at 3,000 m even in July.

reviews.author: Aya S.
reviews.body: We were three beginners. The guides matched horses to each of us and answered every packing question on WhatsApp before the trip.

guides.title: Song-Kul Lake: Yurt Camps, Horse Treks and How to Get There
guides.excerpt: Song-Kul is a high mountain lake at 3,016 m where herder families live in yurts from June to September. Here is when to go, how to get there and what to pack.

hero.alt: Yurt camp and grazing horses on the shore of Song-Kul at sunset

sections.title: What makes Song-Kul special
paragraphs: Song-Kul lies in a wide basin of summer pastures (jailoo) surrounded by mountain ridges. There are no towns or hotels on the shore, only yurt camps that families set up for the summer.
From autumn to late spring the lake is frozen and the passes are closed by snow. In June the herders drive their horses, sheep and cattle up, and the pastures fill with life until September.

sections.title: Best time to visit
paragraphs: The season is short. Camps open in mid-June and close in mid-September; dates move with the weather each year.
bullets: June: camps are being set up, flowers on the pastures, cold nights and possible snow on the passes.
July to mid-August: the warmest days and the busiest camps. The best time for horse treks.
Late August to September: fewer travellers, yellow grass, families start moving down.

sections.title: How to get there
paragraphs: Most trips start in Kochkor, about three hours by road from Bishkek. From Kochkor or Naryn, a 4×4 takes you over one of the passes to the lake, or you ride there in two to three days on horseback.
The road from Naryn climbs the Moldo-Ashuu pass with a long series of hairpin bends. The route from Kochkor goes over the Kalmak-Ashuu pass. Both need a high-clearance vehicle.

sections.title: Where to stay: yurt camps
paragraphs: You sleep in a felt yurt on thick mattresses with heavy blankets. A small stove heats the yurt in the evening. Toilets are simple outhouses; some camps have a solar panel for lights and charging.
Family camps are the simplest and the most personal. A few camps offer beds and more comfort for a higher price.

sections.title: What to pack
paragraphs: Weather changes fast at 3,000 m. Even in July you can get rain, hail and freezing nights.
bullets: Warm layers, a down jacket, hat and gloves
Cash in Kyrgyz som: there are no ATMs or card terminals at the lake

sections.title: Being a good guest
paragraphs: Herder families welcome guests warmly. A few customs go a long way:
bullets: Don't step on the threshold of the yurt.
Accept bread and tea with your right hand or both hands.
Take all your rubbish back with you: there is no waste collection on the pastures.
